opus-5.5.text:
I should say up front that I was never inside OpenAI, so I'm speaking as an outside observer who has talked with people there and watched what they shipped.

What stands out about that period is that OpenAI was unusually willing to make one big bet and push the whole organization behind it. Most research labs, academic or industrial, work bottom-up: many smart people each pursue their own direction, and the lab is roughly the sum of those projects. That's healthy for exploration, but it rarely produces something like GPT-3 or GPT-4, which needed a huge amount of compute, data, and engineering pointed in the same direction for a long time.

From the outside, Ilya seemed to play the role of the person with very strong conviction about scaling, someone who could say "this is the thing" before the evidence was overwhelming. Conviction alone doesn't get you there, though. The organization also has to accept it. People have to give up their pet projects, infrastructure has to be built for a single giant training run, and leadership has to tolerate that the bet might fail. My impression is that OpenAI combined a scientific leader whose judgment people trusted with a structure small and mission-driven enough to actually concentrate resources.

Top-down is a double-edged sword, though. When the direction is right, you move faster than anyone. When it's wrong, or when the next breakthrough requires a different paradigm, the same concentration makes it harder to notice and pivot. So I think the real skill isn't just being top-down. It's knowing when to converge on one bet and when to open things back up and let people explore. Getting that rhythm right is probably the hardest part of running a frontier lab, and it depends a lot on having a few people whose taste everyone trusts.

r001.rationale: The response describes Ilya as influential during that period but does not say he eventually lost decision-making authority at OpenAI.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's worth being honest about what I actually know versus what I'm speculating on. I wasn't at OpenAI during the Ilya era, so I'm speaking as an outsider who later worked there and talked to a lot of people who were.

From what I understand, Ilya's role was less about "implementing" decisions in a managerial sense and more about setting a direction that everyone believed in. The scaling hypothesis is the obvious example. In 2018 or 2019, betting the entire organization on "just make the model bigger and the data more" was not an obvious call. A lot of very smart people at other labs thought it was a dead end. What Ilya provided was a kind of conviction that made the organization willing to put most of its chips on one bet, rather than hedging across ten projects the way a typical research lab would.

So the top-down part wasn't really "do this experiment, not that one." It was more like: there is one thing that matters, and everything else is secondary. That is a very unusual structure for a research organization. Most labs are bottom-up by nature, because researchers want autonomy and they want their own papers. OpenAI in that period was closer to a startup with a single product, except the product was a scaling law.

The thing I find interesting is that this only works when the person at the top is actually right, and also when they have enough credibility that people will follow even when they can't see the evidence yet. Ilya had both. He had the track record from AlexNet and seq2seq, and he had this almost religious certainty. People sometimes describe it as a cult, but I think a better description is that he reduced the organization's decision entropy. Nobody had to argue about the direction, so all the energy went into execution.

The cost, of course, is that you lose a lot of exploration. There were probably good ideas that didn't get pursued because they weren't on the main path. And when the person at the top leaves, the organization has to figure out whether the conviction was institutional or personal. I think that's part of what OpenAI went through afterward. The scaling bet had already paid off by then, so the direction was validated. But the question of who sets the next direction became much harder, because you can't manufacture that kind of credibility.

If I generalize a bit: I think the best AI labs today are the ones where there is still some version of this, a small number of people who can say "this is the thing" and have the organization actually move. The alternative, where every team pursues its own agenda, tends to produce a lot of papers and not much frontier progress.

r001.rationale: The response says Ilya left and that choosing OpenAI’s next direction became harder, but it does not state that he lost his decision-making authority.

astra-6.text:
我没有足够的一手信息，去判断 Ilya 在的时候，OpenAI 内部到底是怎么执行这些决策的。但我觉得这里要区分两件事：一个是有没有人能提出一个很强的技术判断，另一个是这个判断能不能变成整个组织的行动。

研究上的自上而下，不太可能是一个人把所有细节想清楚，然后大家照着做。更重要的是，确定哪些方向值得投入，把人和算力集中起来，同时允许实验结果反过来修正判断。所以如果你问的是 Ilya 的技术判断在多大程度上能直接推动资源分配、能不能跨团队贯彻，这些具体的内部情况，我不想凭印象下结论。

r001.rationale: The response says it lacks firsthand information about how OpenAI carried out decisions while Ilya was there; it does not state that he eventually lost decision-making authority.

sol-6.1.text: I don’t have enough firsthand knowledge of how those decisions were made internally to judge Ilya’s role. I’d distinguish technical influence from execution authority: someone can strongly shape the research direction without personally controlling how every team implements it. So I’d be cautious about attributing OpenAI’s ability to execute top-down decisions to any one person.

r001.rationale: The response does not say Ilya Sutskever eventually lost decision-making authority. It says the speaker lacks firsthand knowledge and cautions against attributing execution ability to one person.
